title: Beyond Good and Evil
idea: Every philosophy as a hidden confession. Nietzsche asks what each value is for, and whom it serves.
alt: Painting: Beyond Good and Evil as one alpine landscape at dusk. A toppled marble bust, a misty chasm, a rose-lit summit above a lake, and a white mask with ultramarine ribbons.

chapters.name: The prejudices of philosophers
chapters.label: Part 1
chapters.note: Every great philosophy, Nietzsche suspects, is a confession of its author: a defence of a prejudice, dressed up as a proof.

chapters.name: The free spirit
chapters.label: Part 2
chapters.note: Whatever is deep wears a mask. The free spirit keeps its distance, its secrets and its laughter.

chapters.name: Epigrams and interludes
chapters.label: Part 4
chapters.note: Aphorisms, among them the famous warning: gaze long into an abyss, and the abyss gazes back into you.

chapters.name: What is noble?
chapters.label: Part 9
chapters.note: Nobility as a rank of the soul: the reverence a person has for themselves, and the distance they keep from the crowd.

title: Twilight of the Idols
idea: Nietzsche's philosophy in miniature, written in about a week: idols sounded out with a hammer and found hollow.
alt: Painting: a blazing noon. Hollow stone idols with a hammer, a clay cup beside a sprig of hemlock, a sundial with almost no shadow, and a vine-grown temple with an ivy staff tied with an ultramarine ribbon.

chapters.name: Foreword
chapters.note: Sounding out idols with a hammer, as with a tuning fork: the hollow ones give themselves away.

chapters.name: The problem of Socrates
chapters.note: The wisest of every age judged life worthless, and Socrates, dying, called it a sickness. Nietzsche asks what that verdict says about the judges.

chapters.name: How the true world became a fable
chapters.note: The history of an error in six short steps, ending at noon, the moment of the shortest shadow.

chapters.name: What I owe to the ancients
chapters.note: Not the Greeks of the philosophers but of Thucydides and Dionysus: realism, and a yes to life.

title: Essays and Aphorisms
idea: The readable Schopenhauer. Life swings between want and boredom, and the short essays on reading, thinking and noise show how to live with it.
alt: Painting: a winter dusk. An hourglass on ultramarine silk, a storm-bent tree on a hill, porcupines huddled in the snow, and the lamplit window of a study.

chapters.name: On the suffering of the world
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Pain is the positive thing in life, Schopenhauer argues, and happiness only its brief absence.

chapters.name: On the vanity of existence
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Time takes everything we hold. The present keeps slipping into the past, which is why nothing in life quite satisfies.

chapters.name: On thinking for oneself
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: Reading is thinking with someone else's head. A little you have thought through beats a library you have only read.

chapters.name: Similes, parables and fables
chapters.label: Essay
chapters.note: The porcupines on a cold day: they huddle for warmth, prick each other, and settle at a polite distance.

title: Letters from a Stoic
idea: Letters to a friend on how to live: time, reading, crowds, fear and friendship, from a statesman who knew power from the inside.
alt: Painting: a villa terrace above the Bay of Naples. A bronze water clock, a few scrolls on ultramarine cloth, an amphitheatre in a haze of dust, and a ship leaving harbour.

chapters.name: On saving time
chapters.label: Letter 1
chapters.note: Hold every hour in your grasp. Of all we have, only time is truly ours, and we let it slip away.

chapters.name: On reading
chapters.label: Letter 2
chapters.note: Stay with a few great writers and digest them. To be everywhere is to be nowhere.

chapters.name: On crowds
chapters.label: Letter 7
chapters.note: Avoid the crowd. Seneca comes home from the midday games more cruel and less human for having watched.

chapters.name: On travel
chapters.label: Letter 28
chapters.note: Travel cures nothing, because you take yourself along. You need a change of soul, not of sky.

title: Republic
idea: What justice is, worked out by building a city in words. And the cave: prisoners who take the shadows on the wall for the world.
alt: Painting: the Republic as one landscape. A firelit cave with shadows on its wall, a ship in the bay, a pillar of rainbow light in the sky, and a gold ring on ultramarine silk.

chapters.name: The ring of Gyges
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible. Would anyone stay just if no one could see?

chapters.name: The ship of state
chapters.label: Book VI
chapters.note: Sailors fight over the helm and mock the one who studies the stars and the winds. Who should steer a city?

chapters.name: The cave
chapters.label: Book VII
chapters.note: Prisoners take the shadows on the wall for the world. One is led up into the sun, and comes back to be laughed at.

chapters.name: The myth of Er
chapters.label: Book X
chapters.note: A soldier comes back from death and tells how souls choose their next lives beneath a pillar of light, like a rainbow.

title: The Nicomachean Ethics
idea: Virtue as a habit rather than a rule: the mean between too much and too little, found by practice and judgement.
alt: Painting: an Aegean morning. An archery target with an arrow in its centre, a level brass balance, two cups on a table under a pergola, and an armillary sphere on a hill.

chapters.name: The good
chapters.label: Book I
chapters.note: Every action aims at some good. The highest is living well, and like archers we do better with a target to aim at.

chapters.name: The mean
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: Virtue is a habit of choosing the mean between too much and too little, found by practice, not by rule.

chapters.name: Friendship
chapters.label: Book VIII
chapters.note: Friends of use and pleasure come and go. Friends who love each other for who they are wish each other good for its own sake.

chapters.name: Contemplation
chapters.label: Book X
chapters.note: The happiest life is the life of the mind: contemplation, the most self-sufficient thing we do.

title: The Odyssey
idea: Ten years to get home: a man of many turns, a household holding out for him, and the long road back to who he was.
alt: Painting: an Aegean morning. A boulder across a cave mouth with sheep grazing, a small rocky island in the surf, a bow beside a row of twelve axe-heads, and a bed built around an olive tree.

chapters.name: The Cyclops
chapters.label: Book IX
chapters.note: Trapped in the Cyclops' cave behind a boulder, Odysseus calls himself Nobody, blinds the giant and escapes beneath the sheep.

chapters.name: The Sirens
chapters.label: Book XII
chapters.note: Odysseus has himself bound to the mast to hear the Sirens sing, while his crew row on with wax in their ears.

chapters.name: The bow and the axes
chapters.label: Book XXI
chapters.note: Penelope's test: string Odysseus's bow and shoot through twelve axe-heads. Only the beggar in the hall can.

chapters.name: The olive-tree bed
chapters.label: Book XXIII
chapters.note: Penelope's last test: their bed cannot be moved, because Odysseus built it around a living olive tree.

title: The Aeneid
idea: The founding poem of Rome: a refugee from burning Troy carries his father and his gods to a new country, at great cost.
alt: Painting: a city burning across the sea with a wooden horse before it, a new harbour city under scaffolding, a golden bough above a dark cave, and huts on a green hill by a river.

chapters.name: Carthage rising
chapters.label: Book I
chapters.note: Shipwrecked, Aeneas watches the Carthaginians building their city and envies them: their walls are already rising.

chapters.name: The fall of Troy
chapters.label: Book II
chapters.note: The wooden horse, the night attack, the city in flames: Aeneas tells Dido how Troy fell.

chapters.name: The golden bough
chapters.label: Book VI
chapters.note: To enter the underworld and meet his father, Aeneas must first break a golden bough from a dark tree.

chapters.name: The site of Rome
chapters.label: Book VIII
chapters.note: Aeneas walks with King Evander over the hills where Rome will stand, still a place of huts and cattle.

title: The Three Theban Plays
idea: Oedipus answers the Sphinx and still cannot see himself. Antigone sets the city’s law against an older one.
alt: Painting: Thebes at evening. A burial mound outside the city walls, a winged sphinx above a plain where three roads meet, and a sacred grove of olive and laurel.

chapters.name: Antigone
chapters.note: Antigone buries her brother against the king's decree, setting the city's law against an older, unwritten one.

chapters.name: Oedipus the King
chapters.note: Oedipus solved the Sphinx's riddle. Now he hunts a killer back to the place where three roads meet, and finds himself.

chapters.name: Oedipus at Colonus
chapters.note: Old, blind and exiled, Oedipus reaches the sacred grove at Colonus, near Athens, where at last he is taken in.

title: Parallel Lives
idea: Paired lives of Greeks and Romans, written to show character in small things: a jest, a gesture, a single decision.

cover.alt: Cover of Makers of Rome, a Penguin Classics selection of Plutarch's Lives

alt: Painting: a temple on a citadel wrapped in scaffolding, a yoke tied with a great knot, a river bridge with an eagle standard, and fresh figs on ultramarine cloth.

chapters.name: Pericles
chapters.note: Pericles turns Athens into a building site, and Plutarch marvels that work done so quickly has lasted so long.

chapters.name: Alexander
chapters.note: At Gordium, Alexander is shown a knot no one can untie, and undoes it his own way.

chapters.name: Cato the Elder
chapters.note: Cato drops fresh figs from Carthage in the Senate, grown three days' sail from Rome. Carthage, he says, must be destroyed.

chapters.name: Caesar
chapters.note: Caesar halts at the Rubicon and weighs the cost for a long while, then says, ‘Let the die be cast’, and crosses.

title: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
idea: Thirteen centuries of how a vast, working system comes apart: slowly, from within, in famously measured prose.
alt: Painting: Rome's history in one view. A golden forum, smoke rising beyond the walls, a domed city across a strait, and a fallen column among ruins.

chapters.name: The age of the Antonines
chapters.label: Chapters 1–3
chapters.note: The empire at its height in the second century: peace, law and prosperity, the happiest age, Gibbon thought, in human history.

chapters.name: Constantinople founded
chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.note: Constantine builds a new capital on the Bosphorus, and the empire's centre of gravity moves east.

chapters.name: Alaric sacks Rome
chapters.label: Chapter 31
chapters.note: In 410 the Goths under Alaric enter Rome, the first time in eight centuries the city has fallen to a foreign enemy.

chapters.name: The ruins of Rome
chapters.label: Chapter 71
chapters.note: The last chapter: Rome in the fifteenth century, its monuments quarried and overgrown, seen from the Capitol.
